analysis.one_liner: Puts unregulated energy and metals derivatives trading under federal anti-fraud and anti-manipulation oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2003, despite 11 senators from both parties sponsoring it.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron collapse, Senator Dianne Feinstein proposed ending the exemption that let energy and metals derivatives trade on electronic platforms with almost no federal oversight. The bill would have put those trades under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules, required trading platforms to keep five years of records, report large positions, publish daily volume and price data, and hold capital against their risk. It was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay energy prices, and honest traders. The bill targeted a market where opaque, unregulated electronic trading had been blamed for price manipulation, such as during the western energy crisis. Anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules, public price and volume data, and capital requirements would make it harder for a few large players to rig prices that consumers ultimately pay, and give regulators the records needed to prove it when they did.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Energy consumers and honest market participants

how_it_helps.text: Places energy and metals derivatives outside the exemption from the Commodity Exchange Act, making them subject to federal prohibitions on cheating, fraud, and market price manipulation [S2][S3].

Requires electronic 'bilateral dealer markets' — the trading systems where these swaps were executed — to notify and file reports with the CFTC, keep transaction records for five years open to regulators and the Justice Department, and publish daily volume, settlement prices, and open interest to the public [S2][S3].
Requires trading platforms to adopt a CFTC-approved risk model and hold capital commensurate with the risk of trades on the platform [S3].
Directs FERC, CFTC, the SEC, the FTC, and the Federal Reserve to meet quarterly on conditions in energy trading markets and any regulatory gaps [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Energy trading firms, merchant energy companies, and electronic trading platforms bear the cost of compliance — recordkeeping, reporting, public data disclosure, and capital requirements. Some of that cost could be passed into energy prices or reduce the convenience of opaque trading that large participants had used.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on energy trading firms and could be passed through to energy prices or push some trading offshore, though the bill explicitly preserves FERC's existing authority over energy transactions rather than adding a duplicate regulator [S3].
Tighter oversight and public disclosure of positions could reduce trading liquidity in energy hedging markets that airlines, utilities, and other businesses use to manage fuel costs.

The quarterly interagency meetings are largely procedural and depend on agencies choosing to act on what they discuss; the bill's practical force comes from the CFTC authority, not the coordination requirement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's consumer protection value was large by design: it aimed to close a specific gap through which energy derivatives had traded with no anti-manipulation oversight, a gap implicated in real price manipulation harming consumers. The costs — compliance burdens on trading firms and some possible loss of market liquidity — are real but modest relative to the harm the bill aimed to prevent. Its interagency coordination provisions are weak by comparison, but the core CFTC authority was substantive.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on July 11, 2002, with ten cosponsors — eight Democrats and two Republicans, including Agriculture Committee Chairman Tom Harkin [S1][S4][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which holds jurisdiction over the Commodity Futures Trading Commission [S5].
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action followed before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].
The exemption this bill targeted had been created by the 2000 Commodity Futures Modernization Act and stayed in place until Congress repealed it in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, eight years later.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy trading firms kept trading energy and metals derivatives outside federal anti-manipulation oversight for another eight years, until the 2010 Dodd-Frank law closed the gap. Consumers and regulators went without the records, public data, and anti-fraud tools this bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its jurisdiction provisions stripping the regulatory exemption for energy and metals derivatives; the bill was referred to committee and went no further [S1][S3][S5].

for.name: 2 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from introduction [S4].

against.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill [S4], but as chairman of the committee of jurisdiction never brought it to a markup, hearing, or vote — the record shows no committee action after the July 11 referral [S5].

against.name: Energy and futures trading industry
against.role: OTC energy derivatives dealers and exchanges that had won the 2000 exemption from CFTC oversight
against.what_they_did: Opposed restoring Commodity Exchange Act jurisdiction over electronic energy trading, having just obtained that exemption in the Commodity Futures Modernization Act.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor roster was bipartisan — 8 of 49 Senate Democrats and 2 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored — but the Senate took no action on the bill in the five-plus months remaining in the session [S4][S5].

industries.industry: OTC energy derivatives dealers (merchant energy firms and hedge funds)
industries.note: The bill removed their exemption from the Commodity Exchange Act, subjecting their trades to federal anti-fraud and anti-manipulation prohibitions with CFTC enforcement. Unregulated opacity in this market had enabled price manipulation that flowed into the prices households and businesses pay.

industries.industry: Electronic energy trading platforms (bilateral dealer markets)
industries.note: Platforms would have had to register with the CFTC, file large-trader reports, keep five years of records open to regulators and the Justice Department, publish daily volume and price data, and hold capital against risk — costs of operating in the open.
Exchanges already operating under CFTC oversight gained a more level playing field, since competing electronic energy markets would have faced similar recordkeeping and anti-fraud rules.
